whatTheyArgued: Clark & Haviland (1977, read in extracted PDF text): under the given-new contract a listener who cannot find an antecedent can build an inferential bridge from something already known (their example is 'John is a Democrat. Bill is honest too.'), draw an implicature, add, or restructure. Grounding and common ground are Clark's later work (Clark & Schaefer 1989; Using Language 1996, not read).

scholarship.ref: Clark & Haviland, 'Comprehension and the given-new contract' (1977), Stanford-hosted PDF
scholarship.supports: bridging as one repair when no direct antecedent exists, the listener's inference, speaker's responsibility for the gap being bridgeable
scholarship.disputes: the text has no car/engine example (searched for 'engine'); the manifest attributes bridging to Clark 1975 and I did not read that

ourUse: affordance-reference.js: 'the engine' resolves only if a named giver has declared a car-affords-engine entry in the hyperlexicon ledger; never from co-occurrence.

bends.ours: Bridge licensed by a ledger entry a named giver declared.
bends.theirs: The listener infers the bridge from what is mutually known, defeasibly, with the speaker answerable for it. Ours is stricter and a different mechanism: no common-ground model exists in the code.

bends.ours: Compendium cites Using Language (1996) for bridging and car/engine.

Common ground in Clark is mutual belief built jointly in conversation; ours is one declared lexical affordance.
